topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

outline.topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Matrix as a Machine
sections.content: Briefly review that a 2x2 matrix acts as a function (linear transformation) that moves points in 2D space. Visualize a 2D grid with a character (e.g., a 'Cyber-Cat') sitting on it. Applying matrix A transforms the cat (e.g., rotates it). Introduce the notation T(v) = Av.
sections.example: A 'Cyber-Cat' at coordinates (1,1) is rotated 90 degrees counter-clockwise by matrix A = [[0, -1], [1, 0]].

sections.title: The Sequential Challenge
sections.content: Introduce the concept of applying two transformations in a row. First, apply transformation A (rotation), then apply transformation B (scaling/stretching). Show the Cyber-Cat rotating first, and then the rotated cat getting stretched. This defines the composition B(A(v)).
sections.example: The rotated Cyber-Cat is now stretched horizontally by matrix B = [[2, 0], [0, 1]]. We see the cat move twice.

sections.title: Finding the Shortcut (The 'Why')
sections.content: Explain the motivation: instead of calculating two separate steps for every point, we want a single 'Master Matrix' C that performs both actions in one leap. This Master Matrix C is the product of B and A (C = BA). Emphasize the right-to-left order of operations.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Teleportation Gate' where the original cat enters and the rotated-then-stretched cat instantly exits on the other side.

sections.title: The Mechanics: Basis Vector Tracking
sections.content: Graphically demonstrate why we multiply 'Rows by Columns'. Follow the basis vectors i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). Show that the columns of matrix BA represent where the basis vectors end up after undergoing transformation A then transformation B.
sections.example: Animate the i-hat vector: first it rotates to (0,1) via A, then it is scaled to (0,1) via B. This tracking forms the first column of the resulting product matrix.

sections.title: Order Matters: Non-Commutativity
sections.content: Use the visual nature of transformations to show why AB is not the same as BA. Changing the order of transformations usually results in a different final position for our character.
sections.example: Compare two scenarios: (1) Rotate then Stretch vs. (2) Stretch then Rotate. Show the Cyber-Cat ending up in two completely different orientations on the grid.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Connection
sections.content: Recap that matrix multiplication is just the mathematical 'glue' that binds multiple geometric steps together. Briefly mention applications in computer graphics (CGI) or robotics where hundreds of transformations are 'baked' into one matrix.
sections.example: A 3D character in a video game moving its arm: the movement is a composition of rotation matrices at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Matrix as a Machine
lecture_lines: A 2x2 matrix acts like a function on space.
It transforms every point in the 2D grid.
We represent this transformation as T(v) = Av.
animations: Show a 2D coordinate grid with a 'Cyber-Cat' shape at (1,1) in #FFFFFF.
Display the matrix A = [[0, -1], [1, 0]] in #00FFFF and formula T(v)=Av in #FFFF00.
Animate the grid and 'Cyber-Cat' rotating 90 degrees counter-clockwise to position (-1,1).

storyboard.title: The Sequential Challenge
lecture_lines: We can apply two linear transformations in sequence.
First, matrix A rotates our character.
Then, matrix B stretches the result.
animations: Start with the rotated 'Cyber-Cat' from the previous step on the grid.
Display matrix B = [[2, 0], [0, 1]] in #00FF00 and the composition formula B(A(v)) in #FFFFFF.
Animate the cat stretching horizontally by a factor of 2, reaching position (-2,1).

storyboard.title: Finding the Shortcut (The 'Why')
lecture_lines: Instead of two steps, we want one "Master Matrix".
The product matrix C performs both transformations at once.
Multiplication order is right-to-left: C = BA.
animations: Display the original 'Cyber-Cat' next to the final transformed cat for comparison.
Introduce the 'Master Matrix' C = BA in #FFA500 as a single shortcut.
Highlight the right-to-left order of B then A in the expression BA using #FF00FF.
Create a 'Teleportation Gate' visual as a glowing #00FFFF rectangle.
Animate the cat entering the gate and instantly exiting in its final rotated-stretched form.

storyboard.title: The Mechanics: Basis Vector Tracking
lecture_lines: To find BA, track the basis vectors.
Watch where i-hat lands after both steps.
Then, track where j-hat ends up.
These final positions form the columns of BA.
This explains the "row by column" rule.
animations: Highlight the basis vector i-hat (1,0) in #FF0000 on the unit grid.
Animate i-hat rotating to (0,1) under transformation A.
Show the rotated i-hat undergoing transformation B (scaling), remaining at (0,1).
Place the final vector (0,1) into the first column of the result matrix C.
Repeat the tracking for j-hat (0,1) to fill the second column of matrix C.

storyboard.title: Order Matters: Non-Commutativity
lecture_lines: In matrix multiplication, the order of operations matters.
Rotating then stretching differs from stretching then rotating.
Matrix AB is usually not equal to BA.
Geometry shows why multiplication is not commutative.
animations: Display two grids side-by-side for Scenario 1 (BA) and Scenario 2 (AB).
In Scenario 1, animate Rotate then Stretch; highlight final cat in #FFD700.
In Scenario 2, animate Stretch then Rotate; highlight final cat in #ADFF2F.
Show the two final cats at different coordinates to demonstrate they are not equal.
Display the inequality AB!= BA in bold #FF0000 at the center.

storyboard.title: Summary and Real-World Connection
lecture_lines: Matrix multiplication glues multiple geometric steps together.
It "bakes" complex movements into a single matrix.
This is essential for CGI and robotics.
animations: Show a sequence of matrices (M3 * M2 * M1) being condensed into one matrix M.
Display a simple line-diagram of a robotic arm with joints in #C0C0C0.
Animate the arm moving smoothly as the product matrix 'bakes' all joint rotations together.
